fr-tarte-au-citron: In a food processor or by hand, combine the flour, icing sugar, and salt. Add the cold cubed butter and pulse until the mixture resembles fine sand — no visible butter chunks. Add the egg yolk and 1–2 teaspoons of cold water and pulse until the dough just comes together. Do not overwork. Press into a flat disc, wrap, and refrigerate for 30 minutes. Roll to 3 mm thickness and line a 22–24 cm fluted tart tin with a removable base. Press gently into the flutes, trim the top neatly, and refrigerate for another 20 minutes. Blind-bake at 180°C (355°F) lined with parchment and weights for 15 minutes, then remove weights and bake a further 10–12 minutes until the base is a uniform pale golden-brown.

In a medium bowl, whisk together the eggs, caster sugar, lemon juice, and lemon zest until the sugar is fully dissolved and the mixture is smooth and uniformly pale yellow. Do not beat to foam — this should be whisked just enough to combine. Set the bowl over a saucepan of barely simmering water (bain-marie), making sure the base of the bowl does not touch the water.

Cook the lemon mixture over the bain-marie, whisking constantly with a flexible spatula or whisk, scraping the sides of the bowl frequently. The mixture will slowly thicken. Continue cooking until it reaches 82°C (180°F) on a thermometer, or the nappe stage: when you draw a finger across the back of a spoon coated in curd, it should leave a clean line. This takes 8–12 minutes. Remove from heat immediately and whisk in the cold butter cubes in two additions, waiting for each to incorporate before adding more. The butter is what makes the curd silky rather than just thick.

Strain the finished warm curd through a fine sieve directly into the cooled tart shell. Gently tap the tin on the counter twice to level the surface and release any air bubbles. Transfer to the refrigerator and chill uncovered for at least 2 hours, or until the curd has set to a sliceable consistency. Serve at room temperature — remove from the fridge 20–30 minutes before serving so the curd softens slightly to its ideal silken texture.

fr-tea-eggs: Place eggs in a single layer in a saucepan. Cover with cold water by 2 cm. Bring to a full boil over medium-high heat. Once boiling, cover and remove from heat. Let stand for exactly 10 minutes, then transfer to an ice bath for 5 minutes. The eggs should be fully hard-boiled with no grey ring at the yolk — they will be simmered further and need to start fully cooked.

Using the back of a spoon, tap each egg all over its surface to create a fine network of cracks through the shell. The goal is to crack the shell without removing it — the shell must stay on to hold its shape during simmering. Cracks should be dense and close-set across the entire surface, like a cracked glaze on a ceramic piece.

Combine the strong black tea, both soy sauces, star anise, cinnamon, cloves, Sichuan peppercorns, sugar, and mandarin peel in a pot large enough to hold all the eggs in one layer. Bring to a simmer and add the cracked eggs. Simmer gently for 20 minutes — the shells should not bounce around. Remove from heat, let cool to room temperature in the liquid, then refrigerate in the braising liquid for a minimum of 4 hours, or overnight for the deepest color and flavor.

Peel each egg under cold running water, removing the shell fragments and the inner membrane together. The revealed surface should show a striking marble pattern: dark brown-black staining along every crack line set against the pale amber of the stained egg white. Serve whole or halved, at room temperature or cold.

fr-tempeh-rendang: Blend the soaked dried chilies, shallots, garlic, ginger, coriander, and cumin into a smooth paste in a food processor or blender. Add a tablespoon of water if needed to get it moving. The paste should be fine-textured, deep brick-red, and smell intensely of raw shallot and warm spice.

Heat coconut oil in a large wok or heavy pot over medium heat. Add the paste and fry, stirring constantly, for 8–12 minutes. The paste will first thin out as moisture evaporates, then darken and deepen in color, and finally begin to separate from the oil — a thin ring of clear oil appears around the paste. This is keluarkan minyak — the oil breaking out. This step develops the foundational flavor.

Add tempeh to the fried paste and stir to coat. Pour in coconut milk, add the lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime leaves, turmeric leaf if using, salt, and palm sugar. Stir to combine. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a medium simmer. Cook uncovered, stirring every 10 minutes to prevent sticking.

Continue simmering uncovered for 1–1.5 hours, stirring every 10 minutes with increasing frequency as the liquid reduces. The coconut milk will pass through several stages: creamy white, then pale yellow, then the coconut fat will separate and the paste will begin to fry in its own oil. This final stage — when the rendang is almost dry and the tempeh is frying in coconut oil — develops the characteristic dark, burnished crust. Keep stirring to prevent scorching. The rendang is done when the tempeh is dark and encrusted and the 'sauce' is more of a thick, dark coating.

Transfer to a serving plate or shallow bowl. Scatter fried shallots over the top. Serve with steamed rice, sambal, and pickled cucumber. Rendang improves overnight — the flavors deepen and the spice coating firms.
fr-tempeh-sambal: Heat 1 cm of oil in a wide skillet over medium-high heat. When the oil shimmers and a small piece of tempeh sizzles immediately on contact, begin frying the tempeh slices in a single layer, without crowding. Fry for 3–4 minutes per side until deep golden-brown and crisp on the outside. The tempeh should not be pale — it needs color for the later glazing step to work properly. Drain on a rack, not paper towels.

In the same pan with the remaining tablespoon of oil, add the shallots and cook over medium heat until golden and beginning to caramelize — about 5 minutes. Add the sliced chiles, garlic, lemongrass, and bay leaves. Stir-fry for 3 minutes until the chiles are softened and fragrant. The shallots should be well beyond translucent — approaching crisp and golden — before the kecap manis is added.

Add the fried tempeh to the sambal base. Pour the kecap manis over everything. Toss vigorously over high heat for 2–3 minutes until the kecap manis caramelizes and coats every piece of tempeh in a dark, glossy glaze. The liquid should reduce completely — the pan should be nearly dry. Season with salt if needed (kecap manis is quite salty already). Remove the lemongrass and bay leaves before serving.

fr-tempura-vegetables: Prepare vegetables: slice sweet potato 6mm thick, clean shiitake and score the caps, top and tail green beans, slice lotus root 5mm thick, cut red pepper into wide strips. Pat all vegetables completely dry — any surface moisture prevents batter adhesion and causes dangerous oil splatter. Dust lightly with flour (the second function flour serves after structural gluten — it acts as a primer for batter adhesion). Keep everything cold until the moment of frying.

This step must be done RIGHT BEFORE frying — never in advance. Combine the egg yolk with the ice-cold sparkling water and stir briefly. Add both flours at once and stir with chopsticks or a fork only 8–10 strokes. The batter must remain lumpy, floury, and obviously under-mixed. Large dry flour streaks are normal and desirable. Do not be tempted to mix until smooth — gluten development is the enemy of tempura.

Heat the oil to exactly 170–175 C (340–345 F) — use a thermometer. Dip each vegetable piece briefly in the batter (let excess drip for just 1 second) and lower into the oil. Fry in small batches to maintain oil temperature — too many pieces cools the oil and produces soggy results. Fry 2–3 minutes until the batter sets to a very pale, almost white-gold. Drain on a rack. Serve within 2 minutes.

fr-thai-basil-chicken: Combine oyster sauce, fish sauce, and dark soy sauce in a small bowl. Stir to blend. Taste — it should be powerfully salty and savory. This sauce goes in fast at high heat, so having it ready before you start is essential. Never season a stir-fry by shaking bottles over a hot wok.

Heat oil in a wok over high heat until smoking. Add garlic and bird's eye chilies together. Fry for 30-45 seconds, stirring constantly — the garlic will begin to golden at the edges and the chilies will turn the oil bright orange-red. Do not let the garlic burn or the dish will be bitter.

Add minced chicken and break it apart with a spatula immediately. Stir-fry on high heat for 2-3 minutes, pressing the chicken flat against the wok to get color rather than steam. When no pink remains, pour the sauce around the edge of the wok (not over the chicken) — it will sizzle and char slightly before mixing in. Toss to coat.

Remove wok from heat (or reduce to minimum). Add holy basil leaves all at once and toss vigorously for 10-15 seconds. The leaves will wilt almost instantly from the residual heat. Do not overcook them — they should be wilted and dark green, not brown and mushy. Plate immediately over jasmine rice with a fried egg on top.

fr-thai-basil-fried-rice: Heat a wok or large heavy skillet over the highest flame until smoke wisps from the surface — 2 minutes minimum. Add 30 g of the oil and swirl immediately. Add the garlic and chilies all at once and stir-fry for 20 seconds until the garlic is gold and the kitchen fills with a sharp, peppery fragrance. Add the ground pork, breaking it up with a spatula. Let it sear undisturbed for 30 seconds, then break and toss. Cook for 2–3 minutes total until no pink remains and the pork has some golden, crumbly edges rather than being pale and steamed.

Add the cold rice to the wok, breaking up any clumps with the spatula before it hits the heat. Pour the fish sauce, oyster sauce, and soy sauce around the edge of the wok (not directly on the rice) so the sauces hit the hot metal and sizzle. Toss everything together vigorously for 2–3 minutes, pressing the rice flat against the wok surface for 20 seconds at a time to allow contact browning, then tossing to redistribute. The goal is every grain coated and slightly toasted, not steamed.

Remove the wok from heat. Add all the holy basil leaves at once and fold them through the rice with 4–5 broad strokes of the spatula. The residual heat of the rice and wok will wilt the basil in 20–30 seconds — you want it collapsed and glossy but not black or slimy. Holy basil wilts much faster than Italian basil and turns bitter if overcooked. The leaves should turn a deep, jewel-like green and release a wave of clove-anise fragrance. Taste and adjust with a few drops more fish sauce if needed.

In a small wok or skillet, heat the remaining 10 g of oil over high heat until it shimmers and just begins to smoke. Crack eggs into the oil and let them fry undisturbed for 60–90 seconds. The whites should blister and puff immediately on contact, forming golden lacey edges while the yolk stays barely set and glossy. Tilt the pan and baste the yolk with hot oil using a spoon. The egg is done when the white is fully set and golden-fringed, the yolk still deep orange and runny. Serve immediately atop the rice.

fr-thai-basil-pork: Combine oyster sauce, fish sauce, soy sauce, and sugar in a small bowl. Stir until the sugar dissolves. Taste and adjust: it should be intensely savory, salty, slightly sweet, and smell powerfully of fermented seafood and caramel. Set beside the stove. In pad kra pao, there is no time for measuring once the wok is hot — everything must be ready before you start.

Heat a wok or large cast-iron pan over the highest possible heat until it begins to smoke. Add the oil and heat for 15 seconds. Add the chilies and garlic simultaneously. Stir-fry, keeping everything moving, for 30-45 seconds. The garlic should be fragrant and just beginning to color at the edges — not burnt. The chilies will release intense capsaicin vapor; ensure ventilation. This step is fast and violent.

Add the ground pork to the wok in one addition. Press it flat against the hot surface and let it sear without stirring for 30-45 seconds until the contact side turns grey-to-caramelized. Then break it up and stir-fry vigorously for 2-3 minutes, pressing and breaking apart any clumps. Pour in the pre-mixed sauce and the water. Continue stir-frying over maximum heat for another minute until the sauce has reduced and coated every piece of meat in a sticky, dark glaze. The pan should sound like it is sizzling furiously — not steaming.

Remove the wok from heat. Add all the holy basil leaves at once and toss rapidly — residual heat will wilt the basil in 15-20 seconds. Holy basil releases its best aroma when it hits heat but is not overcooked: the leaves should be wilted but still intensely fragrant and not uniformly black. Serve immediately over jasmine rice, topped with a fried egg cooked in very hot oil until the edges are crispy and lacy.

fr-thai-fish-cakes: Cut the fish into rough chunks. Pulse in a food processor until the fish breaks down into a coarse paste — approximately 15–20 short pulses. Do not blend to a smooth puree; you want some texture remaining. Add the curry paste, fish sauce, egg, and cornstarch. Pulse 10 more times to combine. Then switch from pulsing to processing: run continuously for 30–45 seconds. The mixture will visibly change — it begins to gather into itself, pulling away from the bowl sides and becoming sticky and elastic. This is the myosin protein network forming, the same mechanism that makes bouncy fish balls. This step is not optional.

Transfer the fish paste to a bowl. Add the kaffir lime leaf chiffonade and sliced beans. Fold in firmly with a spatula — not gently, but with real pressure to distribute the additions without breaking the protein network already developed. At this stage, many Thai cooks slap the mixture against the bowl 10–15 times: lift and throw the paste back into the bowl to drive out air bubbles and further tighten the network. Refrigerate the paste for 15 minutes — chilling makes shaping much easier.

Heat the oil in a wok or deep pan to 175°C (350°F). Wet your palms with cold water. Scoop 2 heaped tablespoons of paste and form into a flat disc 1.5 cm thick and 7 cm diameter — they should look like hockey pucks, not balls. Slide gently into the oil. Fry 4–5 at a time without crowding. Cook 2–3 minutes per side until deep golden-brown all over. The cakes will float and puff slightly as they cook — a good sign. Test one by cutting in half: it should be cooked through with no translucent center and a dense, bouncy interior texture.

Drain on paper towels for 60 seconds only — too long and they cool and lose their crackle. Arrange on a serving plate. Serve immediately with Thai cucumber relish (ajat): thin-sliced cucumber and shallot in sweet vinegar with toasted toasted seeds and coriander. The cool, sharp relish is not optional accompaniment — it is the counterpoint the richness demands.
fr-thai-fish-curry: Spoon 4 tablespoons of the thick cream that has risen to the top of the coconut cream can into a wok or wide pan. Heat over medium-high until it begins to bubble and the cream starts to separate (the oil splits from the solids). Add the red curry paste and fry in the coconut cream for 2-3 minutes, stirring constantly, until the paste darkens slightly, the oil separates fully, and the fragrance fills the kitchen. This frying step in coconut cream is the most important step — do not rush it.

Add the remaining coconut cream and stir to combine with the bloomed paste. Add fish sauce, palm sugar, and torn kaffir lime leaves. Stir and taste — adjust the balance of salty (fish sauce), sweet (palm sugar), and heat (curry paste) until it feels harmonious. Add the Thai eggplant. Simmer for 5-7 minutes until the eggplant is just tender but still holds its shape. The sauce should be rich, slightly thickened, and deeply colored.

Nestle the fish pieces into the simmering curry sauce. Reduce heat to medium-low, cover, and cook for 4-6 minutes depending on thickness. Fish is done when it turns opaque throughout and flakes easily when a fork is pressed gently against the flesh. Do not stir after adding fish — the pieces are delicate and will break apart. Gently baste by spooning sauce over the exposed tops once during cooking.

Remove from heat. Tear in Thai basil leaves and stir gently once. Squeeze lime juice over the top. Taste once more for the final balance of salt, sweet, sour, and heat — this is the moment to adjust. Serve immediately over jasmine rice. The basil must go in off the heat to preserve its anise-clove fragrance.
fr-thai-larb: Place the raw glutinous rice in a dry wok or heavy skillet over medium heat. Toast, stirring constantly, for 5–8 minutes until each grain turns golden-brown and the kitchen fills with a popcorn-like, nutty fragrance. Do not walk away — the transition from golden to burnt takes seconds. Transfer to a mortar or spice grinder and grind to a coarse powder (the texture of fine breadcrumbs). This powder is the secret texture of larb: it absorbs the dressing and gives the dish its characteristic sandy bite.

Heat a wok over high heat until smoking. Add the ground chicken with no oil — the natural fat in the meat is sufficient and oil would cause steaming. Break the meat apart rapidly with a spatula, spreading it thin across the hot wok surface. Cook until just no longer pink, about 3–4 minutes. Do not cook through completely — the residual heat and lime acid will finish it. The goal is barely cooked, still juicy chicken.

Working while the chicken is still very hot (the heat helps the dressing penetrate), add fish sauce, lime juice, dried chili flakes, and sugar. Toss vigorously. Taste immediately — the balance is the dish. It should hit sour first, then salty, then heat building at the back of the throat. Adjust: more lime for brightness, more fish sauce for depth, more chili for fire.

Fold in the shallots, mint, cilantro, scallion, and minced lemongrass. Scatter the toasted rice powder over the top and fold in gently — you want it distributed but not completely buried. Taste one final time. Serve immediately on a plate lined with cabbage leaves, with extra mint and raw vegetables on the side. Larb deteriorates quickly as the herbs wilt and the rice powder hydrates — this is a dish that lives in the moment.
fr-toasted-farro-salad: Place the farro in a large dry skillet over medium heat. Toast, stirring constantly, for 4–6 minutes until the grains smell nutty and are golden — some grains may lightly pop. This step is optional but transforms the flavor dramatically. The toasted grains will have a nuttier, more complex flavor after cooking.

Transfer toasted farro to a pot. Cover with generously salted water or stock (3 parts liquid to 1 part farro by volume). Bring to a boil, reduce to a steady simmer, and cook uncovered for 30–40 minutes for whole farro (20–25 for semi-pearled) until the grains are tender but still have a distinct chew — al dente, like a well-cooked barley. Drain any excess liquid.

Toss all the vegetables with a generous amount of olive oil, salt, and chili flakes on a large sheet pan. Spread in a single layer — do not crowd or they will steam. Roast at 220 C (425 F) for 25–30 minutes, turning once halfway, until caramelized and charred at the edges — particularly the cherry tomatoes, which should burst and concentrate.

While both the farro and vegetables are still warm, combine them in a large bowl. Drizzle with remaining olive oil and lemon juice. Add lemon zest, chili flakes, parsley, mint, and toasted nuts. Toss together gently — you want the warm farro to absorb the lemon and oil. Taste and adjust salt, acid, and oil. The salad is excellent warm, but also very good at room temperature.

The salad is excellent warm, but also very good at room temperature.
fr-torta-caprese: If using whole blanched almonds, pulse them in a food processor until they reach a fine, sandy consistency — the texture of coarse cornmeal. Do not over-process: if the almonds become warm and clumping, they are releasing their oils and will turn to almond paste rather than flour. Work in short 3-second pulses, scraping down the sides between each. The goal is a dry, free-flowing nut meal. If using store-bought almond flour, skip this step.

Combine the chopped dark chocolate and butter cubes in a heatproof bowl. Melt together over a gentle bain-marie (a saucepan of barely simmering water, bowl sitting above but not touching the water) or in a microwave in 30-second bursts, stirring between each. The mixture should be completely smooth and glossy — no streaks of unmelted chocolate. Let cool to room temperature, about 10 minutes. Do not use the chocolate mixture while it is still hot, as it will cook the egg yolks in the next step.

Separate the eggs, placing the yolks in one large bowl and the whites in another clean bowl. To the yolks, add the caster sugar and whisk until pale, slightly thickened, and the sugar is mostly dissolved, about 2 minutes. Add the cooled chocolate-butter mixture and whisk to combine. Add the vanilla extract and salt. Fold in the almond flour with a spatula until fully incorporated. The batter will be thick, glossy, and dense. Set aside. In the separate clean bowl, whisk the egg whites with a pinch of salt until they reach soft peaks — they should hold a peak that droops gently at the tip. Gently fold one-third of the whites into the chocolate batter to loosen it, then fold in the remaining whites in two additions, using slow, sweeping strokes to preserve as much air as possible.

Butter and line a 22 cm (9-inch) springform pan with parchment. Pour the batter in and smooth the top gently with a spatula. Bake at 170 C (340 F) for 30-35 minutes. The cake is done when the top is set and cracked, the edges are firm, but the center still has a very slight wobble when the pan is gently shaken — like a barely-set jelly. A toothpick inserted into the center should come out with a few moist crumbs, not wet batter and not clean. The torta caprese is meant to be slightly underbaked by classical standards — the dense, fudgy center is a feature, not an error.

Allow the cake to cool completely in the pan on a wire rack — at least 1 hour, ideally 2. It will firm up significantly as it cools. Do not try to unmold it warm. Once completely cool, unmold from the springform. The cake is deliberately flat, dense, and cracked on top — this is correct and beautiful. Just before serving, dust generously with icing sugar through a fine-mesh sieve for the classic snowfall effect. Serve at room temperature cut in wedges — a warm knife (run under hot water and wiped dry) makes the cleanest cuts.
fr-tortilla-espanola: Pour the olive oil into a heavy 24 cm (9-inch) non-stick or well-seasoned cast-iron skillet — there should be enough oil to submerge the potato and onion slices at least halfway. Heat over medium-low until the oil shimmers lazily. Add the potato slices and onion together with a generous pinch of salt. The oil should surround them in a gentle, slow bubble — this is a confit, not a fry. Adjust heat so the bubbling is slow and the potatoes cook through without browning. Turn the mixture occasionally with a slotted spoon. After 20–25 minutes the potatoes will be completely tender, the onion will have turned translucent and sweet, and both will yield without resistance when pressed. Use a slotted spoon to transfer them to a colander set over a bowl, reserving the precious oil. Let them drain and cool for 5 minutes.

Crack the eggs into a large bowl and beat well with a fork — not a whisk — until the yolks and whites are fully combined. Season with salt. Add the drained, slightly cooled potato and onion to the beaten egg and fold gently together. Do not simply dump and stir: layer the potatoes into the egg, turning the mixture over a few times so the slices separate and are coated individually without breaking into mush. Press the mixture down so the egg covers the potatoes. Rest for 5 minutes — this allows the egg to penetrate between the potato layers and the potato starch to begin thickening the egg slightly, which is what gives corn tortilla its distinctive dense-yet-custardy texture.

Return 2 tablespoons of the reserved olive oil to the skillet and heat over medium until it shimmers. Pour in the egg-potato mixture and immediately shake the pan to spread it evenly. Reduce heat to medium-low and cook undisturbed for 5–6 minutes. Run a flexible spatula around the edge every minute or so to prevent sticking. The corn tortilla is ready to flip when the edges have set firm and turned pale gold, and the center — while still visibly wet and jiggly — no longer sloshes when you shake the pan. The underside should be a deep, even gold. This is the moment of the flip.

Place a flat plate or lid (at least as wide as the pan) over the skillet. In one confident motion, invert the skillet so the corn tortilla falls onto the plate with the cooked side facing up. Add a drizzle of the reserved oil to the pan and slide the corn tortilla back in, uncooked side down. Cook for another 3–4 minutes over medium-low. The ideal corn tortilla espanola is set on the outside and slightly runny — cuajada por fuera, jugosa por dentro — just set outside, juicy within. To check doneness, press the center gently: it should feel like a firm jelly — solid but with a slight give. Slide onto a board or plate and rest 10 minutes before slicing. Corn tortilla improves dramatically at room temperature and is traditionally served between 45 minutes and 3 hours after cooking.
fr-tournedos-rossini: Cut the bread into rounds the exact width of the tournedos so the meat sits flush. Heat clarified butter in a skillet over medium heat and fry the rounds, turning once, until evenly golden and crisp on both faces but still tender at the centre, 1-2 minutes a side. Drain on paper and keep warm — these crisp pedestals lift the meat off its juices so the bottom never goes soggy.

Pat the tournedos bone-dry and season well with salt and pepper. In a heavy skillet, heat a film of clarified butter until shimmering. Sear the filets undisturbed until a deep crust forms, about 3 minutes, then turn and sear the second face, basting, to a rosy medium-rare (52°C / 125°F internal), 3-4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate, tent loosely, and rest while you build the sauce in the same pan. Leave the fond behind.

Score the chilled foie gras slices lightly in a crosshatch and season with salt and pepper. Wipe the skillet of all but a whisper of fat and set over medium-high heat. Sear the foie straight from the fridge, 45-60 seconds per side, until a caramel crust forms but the centre stays just-set and meltingly soft. Lift it out the instant it yields — foie gras renders to nothing if it lingers. Pour off the rendered fat, reserving it, and keep the pan for the sauce.

Lower the heat to medium and sweat the minced shallot in a teaspoon of the reserved foie fat until soft and translucent, about 1 minute. Pour in the Madeira to deglaze, scraping the fond loose, and reduce until syrupy and nearly dry, 2-3 minutes. Add the demi-glace and the minced portion of the truffle and simmer until the sauce coats the back of a spoon and turns deep and glossy, 3-4 minutes.

Off the heat, swirl the cold butter into the sauce a cube at a time until it turns silky and emulsified — never let it boil or it will break. Taste and adjust salt. Set each foie-crowned filet on its crouton, spoon the glossy Madeira sauce over and around, shower with the remaining shaved truffle, and finish with a pinch of fleur de sel. Serve at once, while the foie is still warm and yielding.

fr-tres-leches-cake: Separate the eggs carefully — no trace of yolk in the whites. Beat the yolks with 2 parts of the sugar using an electric mixer on high speed for 4–5 minutes until the mixture is pale yellow, thick, and falls from the beaters in a wide, slow ribbon. In a separate clean bowl, beat the egg whites to soft peaks, then gradually add the remaining sugar and beat to stiff, glossy peaks. The whites must be beaten in a completely grease-free bowl — any fat will prevent them from reaching full volume.

Sift the flour and baking powder directly over the egg foam. Using a large rubber spatula, fold in three additions: cut down the center, sweep along the bottom, and roll the batter up and over the top. Rotate the bowl a quarter turn with each stroke. Work quickly but gently — you are trying to keep every air bubble you spent 5 minutes creating. Thirty strokes maximum. Some unmixed streaks are acceptable; overmixing is not.

Pour the batter into a greased and floured 9x13-inch baking pan. Smooth the top gently. Bake at 175 C (350 F) for 22–28 minutes until the top is golden and a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean. Do not open the oven in the first 20 minutes — the foam structure is fragile until set. Allow to cool in the pan for 10 minutes, then use a wooden skewer or fork to poke holes across the entire surface — rows spaced 2 cm apart, going all the way to the pan bottom. The holes are the highway for the milk soak.

Whisk together the sweetened condensed milk, evaporated milk, 1 part of the heavy cream, and vanilla extract into the three-milk mixture. While the cake is still warm in the pan, slowly pour the entire mixture over the surface in a steady, even stream. Start at the edges and work toward the center. The cake will appear saturated — keep pouring. Some will pool at the sides; use a spoon to redistribute. Refrigerate for a minimum of 2 hours, or overnight. The cold temperature allows the proteins in the milk to set and the sponge to become uniformly saturated rather than soggy.

In a cold bowl (chill it in the freezer for 10 minutes), beat the remaining heavy cream and powdered sugar with an electric mixer on medium-high speed. Start on medium to build structure, increase to high once the cream begins to thicken. Beat to medium-firm peaks — the cream should hold its shape when the beaters are lifted but still be smooth and spreadable, not grainy. Spread evenly over the chilled, soaked cake in a generous layer.

Dust the whipped cream surface evenly with ground cinnamon using a fine-mesh sieve for an even layer. Slice with a clean knife wiped between each cut. Serve cold — this cake is best between 4 C and 8 C (39–46 F). Each slice should be placed on a plate with its full column of soaked cake visible from the side, showing the distinct layers of cake and cream.

fr-tteokbokki: Combine the anchovy stock, gochujang, gochugaru, sugar, and soy sauce in a wide, shallow pan or skillet. Whisk together over medium heat until the gochujang is fully dissolved and the sauce is uniform. Bring to a gentle simmer. Taste — the raw sauce should be aggressively hot, sweet, and savory, slightly more intense than you want the final dish, as the rice cakes will absorb and dilute it.

If using refrigerated rice cakes, soak them in warm water for 10 minutes first to soften. Add the rice cakes and fish cake strips to the simmering sauce. Cook over medium heat, stirring frequently to prevent sticking, for 8 to 12 minutes until the rice cakes are tender all the way through. The sauce will thicken significantly as the starch from the rice cakes is released into it.

Scatter the sliced green onions over the pan in the final 30 seconds of cooking and stir once to incorporate. The sauce at this point should be thick, glossy, and cling to every piece in a heavy coat. Remove from heat immediately — the residual heat of the pan will continue cooking the contents. Serve directly from the pan with toothpicks or chopsticks.

fr-tuna-poke-bowl: Using an extremely sharp knife, cut the ahi tuna against the grain into uniform 2cm cubes. Use a single slicing motion — do not saw back and forth, which tears the flesh and damages the texture. Keep the tuna cold until the moment of mixing; place the cubed pieces on a plate in the refrigerator if working ahead. Uniformity of cut is important both aesthetically and for consistent marination.

In a bowl, combine soy sauce, sesame oil, green onions, sesame seeds, and sriracha. Taste the marinade on its own — it should be salty, nutty, and have a pleasant background heat. Add the cold tuna cubes and fold gently using a rubber spatula. Do not stir aggressively. Marinate for 10-15 minutes in the refrigerator. Do not exceed 20 minutes — the soy will begin to cure the tuna, changing its texture from silky to firmer and darkening the color.

Divide warm rice between bowls and pack it into a smooth mound on one side. Spoon the marinated tuna over half the rice. Fan avocado slices on the opposite side. Place cucumber alongside. Drape a few strips of nori over the tuna. Drizzle any remaining marinade from the bowl over everything. The temperature contrast of warm rice and cold tuna is an essential part of the dish — the rice warms the tuna from below as you eat.

fr-tuna-tataki: Place the tuna in the freezer for 30–40 minutes before searing. Very cold tuna sears faster without cooking the interior — the goal is maximum exterior heat, minimum interior cook. The tuna should feel hard at the surface but not frozen solid. Remove and immediately season all four long sides with salt and pepper.

Heat a cast iron or stainless steel pan over maximum heat for 3 minutes until smoking — test by flicking a drop of water (should vaporize instantly). Add oil in a thin film. Sear the tuna block for exactly 30–45 seconds per side on all four long sides, moving it with tongs. Do not sear the ends. The tuna must never rest stationary long enough to cook through. Work quickly.

Transfer the seared tuna immediately to a cold plate or rest over a small bowl of ice for 2 minutes to halt carryover cooking. Using a very sharp, thin-bladed knife (yanagiba or slicing knife), slice the tuna into 5 mm thick slices in one smooth, drawing motion — never saw. Arrange slices in a single overlapping layer on a cold plate.

Drizzle ponzu over and around the slices. Spoon a small mound of grated ginger onto each slice or place at the side. Drizzle sesame oil in a thin stream. Scatter green onion and sesame seeds. Add daikon alongside if using. A few drops of yuzu juice at the very end brighten everything. Serve immediately.
fr-turkey-white-bean-chili: Heat oil in a 5–6 litre Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Add the turkey in a flat layer, season with half the salt, and leave it alone 4–5 minutes until the underside browns. Break it into small crumbles and cook 3–4 minutes more until no pink remains. Transfer to a bowl, leaving the fat behind.

Reduce heat to medium. Add onion, poblanos, and jalapeño with the rest of the salt and cook 8 minutes, scraping up the browned bits, until soft. Add garlic, cumin, coriander, and oregano and stir 1 minute until fragrant.

Add green chiles, beans, stock, and the turkey with its juices. Bring to a boil, then simmer uncovered 25–30 minutes, stirring occasionally. Mash about a quarter of the beans against the side of the pot to thicken. The chili must return to a full simmer, so the turkey is well past 165°F (74°C).

Stir the masa slurry into the simmering chili and cook 5 minutes, stirring, until it thickens and the raw corn taste cooks out. Off the heat, add lime juice and adjust salt. Serve with cilantro, scallions, and sour cream. To freeze: cool in shallow containers, refrigerate within 2 hours, and freeze up to 4 months; reheat to a full simmer (165°F / 74°C) and refresh with lime.
fr-turkey-zucchini-meatballs-marinara: Toss the grated zucchini with 1/2 tsp of the kosher salt in a colander and let stand 10 minutes. Gather it in a clean kitchen towel and wring out firmly over the sink until most of the liquid is gone — you should lose roughly a third of its weight.

In a large bowl, combine the drained zucchini, panko, beaten egg, Parmesan, grated garlic, oregano, the remaining 1 tsp kosher salt and several grinds of pepper; stir into a paste and let the panko hydrate for 2 minutes. Add the turkey and mix gently with your hands just until evenly combined. With wet hands, roll into 16 balls about 4 cm (1 1/2 inches) across.

Heat 2 tbsp of the olive oil in a 12-inch (30 cm) skillet over medium-high heat. Add the meatballs and brown on at least two sides, turning gently with tongs, 5–6 minutes total. They do not need to be cooked through. Transfer to a plate.

Reduce the heat to medium, add the remaining oil and the sliced garlic and cook 1 minute until fragrant and barely golden. Add the pepper flakes, then the crushed tomatoes and a pinch of salt; bring to a simmer, scraping up the fond. Return the meatballs and any juices, cover partially, and simmer gently 12–15 minutes, turning once, until the sauce thickens and the meatballs reach 165°F (74°C) in the center — the safe temperature for ground poultry.
Tear the basil over the pan, taste the sauce and adjust the salt, and serve with extra Parmesan over pasta, polenta or with crusty bread.

fr-turkish-cilbir: Mince the garlic to a smooth paste with the flat of a knife and a pinch of salt — chop, then smear and drag the blade repeatedly until no chunks remain. Stir it into the yogurt with the remaining salt. Beat until completely smooth. The yogurt must be at room temperature before serving — cold yogurt on hot eggs creates an unpleasant thermal shock and mutes the garlic. Spread it onto the plate now and let it temper while you poach the eggs.

Fill a wide saucepan with at least 8 cm of water. Add the white wine vinegar — the acid tightens the egg white around the yolk. Bring to just below a simmer: small bubbles rising from the bottom, surface barely trembling at 80–85°C. Crack each egg individually into a small cup. Create a gentle whirlpool in the water with a spoon. Slide one egg into the center of the whirlpool; the rotation wraps the white around the yolk. Cook 3–3.5 minutes for a runny yolk. Remove with a slotted spoon, blot the underside on a folded cloth, and place directly onto the yogurt.

In a small saucepan or butter warmer, melt the butter over medium heat until it foams. The moment the foam subsides and the butter turns a deep golden amber, remove from heat and immediately add the Aleppo pepper — it will sizzle and bloom in the hot fat. Swirl the pan. Work fast: the residual heat continues cooking the butter, and Aleppo scorches quickly. The butter should turn a vivid red-orange and smell smoky, sweet, and fragrant.

The eggs are already on the yogurt. Pour the sizzling Aleppo butter directly over the eggs and yogurt — it will pool and seep into the white yogurt, creating rivers of deep red. Scatter fresh dill fronds over everything. Serve immediately with gluten-free flatbread or gluten-free bread on the side for scooping. The temperature contrast is the whole point: cold yogurt beneath, hot egg above, sizzling butter cascading over.
fr-turkish-roasted-vegetables: Preheat oven to 220°C (430°F) with a large sheet tray inside. Toss all cut vegetables and the unpeeled garlic cloves with the olive oil and salt in a large bowl. Spread in a single layer on the hot tray — crowding causes steaming. Roast for 25–30 minutes, turning once halfway, until the edges are deeply caramelized and the zucchini and eggplant have collapsed and charred in patches.

While the vegetables are still warm, squeeze the roasted garlic from their skins directly over the vegetables and stir gently to break them into the mix. Drizzle the pomegranate molasses over and sprinkle the sumac. Toss gently to coat without breaking up the vegetables further. Scatter the fresh mint and parsley. Taste for salt and acidity — the dressing should be assertively tart.

Spread the cold yogurt in a generous layer on the base of a wide serving plate, creating a swoosh with the back of a spoon. Pile the warm dressed vegetables directly onto the yogurt. The contrast of cold, tangy yogurt and warm, sweet-tart vegetables is the heart of the dish. Serve immediately.
fr-vichyssoise: Melt butter in a heavy saucepan over medium-low heat. Add the sliced leeks and a generous pinch of salt. Sweat gently for 10–12 minutes, stirring occasionally, until completely soft, translucent, and sweet-smelling. Do not allow the leeks to color — the finished soup should be ivory-white. Use a lid for the first 5 minutes to steam them faster without browning.

Add the cubed potatoes and pour in the warm stock. Bring to a simmer and cook for 20–25 minutes until the potatoes are completely tender throughout. Do not rush with high heat — a gentle simmer preserves the clean, delicate flavors. The liquid will turn very slightly cloudy as potato starch is released.

Use an immersion blender directly in the pot, or carefully transfer in batches to a stand blender (never fill more than half full with hot liquid). Blend for at least 2 minutes until completely smooth. Pass through a fine-mesh sieve, pressing firmly with a ladle to extract all the liquid and force the vegetable pulp through. Stir in the cold double cream. This sieving step is non-negotiable for the characteristic silky vichyssoise texture.

Transfer the blended soup to a container and refrigerate for at least 1 hour, ideally 4 hours or overnight. Cold temperatures transform the soup — the flavors deepen and meld, and the texture firms slightly to a richer, more velvety consistency. Before serving, taste again — cold soup always needs more salt than warm soup. Adjust seasoning. Serve in chilled bowls with finely snipped chives.
fr-vietnamese-caramel-fish: In a clay pot or small heavy saucepan over medium heat, add the sugar in an even layer without stirring. Watch as the sugar at the edges begins to melt and turn amber (about 3 minutes). Only then tilt the pan gently to encourage even melting — do not stir with a spoon or it will crystallize. Cook until the caramel is a deep mahogany-brown (not black) and smells of bitter toffee. This is the defining flavor of kho tộ — a dark, slightly bitter caramel that balances the salty fish sauce.

Pour the fish sauce into the hot caramel (spatter warning!). Add the coconut water and stir — the mixture will bubble intensely and the caramel will seize before re-dissolving. Add the shallots, garlic, ginger, chili, and black pepper. Lay the catfish steaks in the pot in a single layer, spooning the caramel sauce over. Cover and braise over medium-low heat for 15 minutes, turning the fish once at the 8-minute mark.

Uncover the pot and increase heat to medium-high. Simmer the sauce, basting the fish continuously with a spoon, for 5–8 minutes until the sauce has reduced to a thick, dark, syrupy glaze that coats every surface of the fish. The pot will begin to sizzle more intensely as the water evaporates. Remove from heat. Scatter green onion over the top. Serve directly from the clay pot with steamed jasmine rice.
fr-vietnamese-caramel-pork: Place a clay pot or heavy-bottomed pot over medium heat. Add the white sugar in a thin, even layer. Watch carefully without stirring — as the edges begin to melt and turn amber (about 4–5 minutes), tilt the pan to distribute. When the sugar is fully liquid and the color of dark mahogany, with thin wisps of smoke just beginning, remove from heat immediately.

Add the pork belly pieces to the hot caramel and stir quickly to coat. Stand back — the fat will cause violent sputtering. Sear the pork in the caramel for 3–4 minutes, turning with tongs, until each piece is coated in the dark caramel and beginning to brown.

Add shallots and garlic to the pot and stir for 1 minute. Pour in coconut water and fish sauce — the liquid will seize and splatter as it hits the caramel, then rapidly dissolve it. Add palm sugar and black pepper. Bring to a boil, skim any foam, then reduce to the lowest possible simmer. Cover and cook for 45 minutes.

After 45 minutes, add the peeled hard-boiled eggs. Gently turn them to coat in the broth. Cook uncovered for another 20–25 minutes, occasionally spooning broth over the pork, until the broth has reduced to a glossy, syrupy sauce and the fat on the pork is completely tender and translucent.
Ladle pork, eggs, and sauce into bowls or onto a platter. Scatter green onions and optional chili over the top. Serve immediately with steamed jasmine rice and pickled daikon.
fr-vietnamese-pork-meatballs: Combine ground pork, minced shallots, garlic, fish sauce, sugar, and pepper in a large bowl. Mix with your hands for 2-3 minutes using a squeezing, folding motion — not stirring. The mixture should become slightly sticky and cohesive. The fat should begin to emulsify with the lean meat. Refrigerate for 30 minutes to firm.

Dissolve sugar in warm water. Add fish sauce, lime juice, sliced garlic, and chili. Stir and taste — the broth should land in four-part harmony: salty, sweet, sour, and funky, with no single note dominating. This is the dipping broth that the cooked patties will rest in, so it needs to be slightly more intense than you would drink — the meat will dilute it.

Form the chilled pork into flat, palm-sized patties about 3/4 inch thick (or small round meatballs for gluten-free bun cha proper). Grill over high charcoal heat or a screaming hot cast-iron grill pan. Cook 3-4 minutes per side without moving — you want aggressive charring, not steaming. The fat will drip, flare, and add smoke flavor. Authentic gluten-free bun cha has black char marks and a caramelized exterior.

Transfer the hot grilled patties directly into the bowls of nuoc cham broth. Serve with a plate of fresh herbs, vermicelli rice noodles on the side, and extra chili. The patties will continue steaming in the broth, picking up the sour-sweet nuoc cham and tempering the smoke. This is meant to be eaten immediately, scooping rice noodles into the broth bowl at the table.
fr-vitello-tonnato: Tie the veal with kitchen twine into a compact cylinder if needed. Place in a pot just large enough to hold it. Add white wine, bay leaves, peppercorns, and cold water to cover by 3 cm. Bring very slowly to a bare simmer — 80–85 C, when tiny bubbles rise lazily and the surface barely shivers. Poach for 45–60 minutes, maintaining this temperature throughout. Do not let it boil; boiling will tighten and toughen the veal. Probe with an instant-read thermometer: pull at 62–63 C internal. Let cool completely in the poaching liquid.

Combine the drained tuna, capers, and egg yolks in a blender or food processor. Blend until smooth. With the motor running, add the olive oil in a thin, steady stream — exactly as you would build a mayonnaise — until the sauce is thick, creamy, and pale. Add lemon juice and blend again. Taste: it should be powerfully savory, bright with lemon, and rich enough to coat a spoon thickly. Thin with a tablespoon of poaching liquid if needed for a more draping consistency.

Remove the completely cold veal from the poaching liquid. Using the sharpest knife available, slice the veal as thinly as possible — ideally 2–3 mm, almost translucent. A meat slicer is ideal but a long, thin-bladed knife works if the veal is cold enough (refrigerate for 1 hour before slicing). Each slice should be near-transparent at the edges and nearly white throughout.

Spoon a pool of tonnato sauce onto a large, flat platter. Layer the veal slices overlapping over the sauce. Drizzle more tonnato generously over the top, making sure every slice is covered. Scatter capers and lemon slices decoratively. Refrigerate for at least 1 hour before serving — the sauce must be very cold and the veal must absorb its flavor.
fr-white-bean-kale-parmesan-soup: Warm the olive oil in a 5–6 litre pot over medium-low heat. Add onion, carrot, and celery with a pinch of salt and cook gently 10–12 minutes, stirring now and then, until soft and sweet but not browned. Add garlic, pepper flakes, and the rosemary sprigs and cook 1–2 minutes until the garlic turns pale gold at the edges.

Add beans, Parmesan rind, and stock. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a low simmer and cook uncovered 25–30 minutes, stirring the bottom occasionally so the softened rind doesn't stick. Fish out the rosemary stems. Scoop about 2 cups of beans and liquid into a bowl, mash smooth with a fork or blitz with an immersion blender, and stir back in to thicken the body.

Stir in the kale and simmer 5–8 minutes until tender. Remove the rind (chop any soft parts and return them). Off the heat, add lemon juice and half the grated Parmesan; season with salt and plenty of pepper. Serve with the rest of the cheese and a thread of olive oil. To freeze: cool quickly in shallow containers, refrigerate within 2 hours, and freeze up to 3 months; the soup thickens on standing, so thin with water when reheating and refresh with lemon.
fr-wild-mushroom-risotto: In a wide pan over high heat, melt a small knob of butter until foaming subsides. Add mushrooms in a single layer and cook without moving for 2–3 minutes until deeply browned. Season with salt, toss once, and cook 1 minute more. Remove and set aside. The mushrooms must be seared separately to drive off moisture and develop flavour — adding them directly to the risotto results in grey, steamed fungi.

In a heavy-bottomed wide pot over medium heat, melt half the butter and soften the shallots for 3–4 minutes until translucent. Add the dry rice and stir constantly for 2 minutes until every grain is coated in fat and the grains turn from chalky white to slightly translucent at the edges. You should hear a gentle clicking sound as the grains catch the bottom. This tostatura is essential — it seals the starch so the rice absorbs liquid gradually rather than all at once.

Pour the white wine into the toasted rice and stir vigorously. Cook until fully absorbed, about 2 minutes. Then add warm stock one ladle at a time (roughly 100ml), stirring constantly and waiting for each addition to be almost fully absorbed before adding the next. Keep the stock hot in a separate saucepan throughout. This process takes 18–20 minutes total — do not rush it with large additions of cold stock.

Remove the pot from the heat entirely. Add the seared mushrooms, then vigorously stir in the cold cubed butter and the grated Parmigiano all at once, using a wooden spoon or silicone spatula in a rapid figure-eight motion for 1–2 minutes. This mantecatura is what creates the signature wave-like, all'onda consistency. The cold butter emulsifies with the starchy cooking liquid into a glossy, rich sauce. Serve immediately on warm (not hot) plates.
fr-winter-vegetable-minestrone: Heat the oil in a 6–7 litre pot over medium-low heat. Add onion, carrot, and celery with a pinch of the salt and cook 12–15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until very soft and lightly golden. Add garlic, rosemary, and pepper flakes for 1 minute, then stir in the tomato paste and cook 2 minutes until it darkens.

Add tomatoes, water or stock, Parmesan rind, and the remaining salt; bring to a boil. Add squash and beans and simmer uncovered 25–30 minutes, stirring the bottom now and then, until the squash is tender and some cubes have started to break down into the broth.

Stir in the cabbage and simmer 10 minutes until silky and tender. Remove the rosemary stem and the Parmesan rind (chop any soft bits and return them). Taste for salt. If freezing, stop here: portion off what you'll freeze before adding pasta.

Bring the soup to a lively simmer, add the pasta, and cook 1–2 minutes longer than the package time, stirring often, until tender. Add water if it gets too thick. Serve with grated Parmesan and a drizzle of olive oil. To freeze: cool the pasta-free soup in shallow containers, refrigerate within 2 hours, and freeze up to 3 months; reheat to a simmer and cook fresh pasta right in it.

fr-xiao-long-bao: If making from scratch: simmer pork skin (or trotters) with water, ginger, and scallion for 2–3 hours. Strain, season, and pour the liquid into a flat tray to set in the refrigerator for at least 2 hours until completely firm. The gel should be solid enough to dice. Cut into 1 cm cubes when needed for the filling. If using gelatin: bloom, dissolve in hot pork stock, season, pour into a tray and refrigerate until firm.

Combine ground pork, minced ginger, scallions, soy sauce, Shaoxing wine, salt, sugar, white pepper, and sesame oil in a bowl. Using chopsticks or your hand, stir and fold in one direction only for 3–4 minutes until the mixture becomes sticky and cohesive — the protein strands are aligning. Do not overmix or the filling becomes dense. Refrigerate 30 minutes.

Pour boiling water gradually over the flour while stirring quickly with a fork or chopsticks. Once cool enough to handle (about 2 minutes), knead by hand for 8–10 minutes until the dough is smooth, elastic, and slightly tacky but not sticky. The hot water gelatinizes the starch, making the dough extensible enough to roll paper-thin without tearing. Cover and rest 30 minutes.

Divide the dough into small pieces (about 10g each). Roll each piece into a thin disc 8–9 cm across — thinner at the edges, slightly thicker in the center to resist the soup weight. Place 1 tsp pork filling in the center with 2–3 aspic cubes. Pleat the edges with 18–22 folds, twisting and pinching the top closed. The pleat count is not vanity — more pleats means a tighter seal and less soup loss.

Line bamboo steamer with parchment or cabbage leaves. Place dumplings 2 cm apart — they expand. Steam over vigorously boiling water for exactly 8 minutes. Not 6 (filling undercooked), not 10 (skin tears). Serve immediately in the steamer. Accompany with Chinkiang black vinegar and thin-cut ginger.

fr-yorkshire-pudding: Measure flour and salt into a large bowl and make a well in the centre. Crack the eggs into the well and whisk them into the flour gradually, pulling in flour from the edges until a thick, lump-free paste forms — this is critical, because lumps introduced at the end never fully smooth out. Once the paste is smooth, pour in the milk in a thin stream, whisking constantly. The finished batter should be the consistency of single cream and absolutely smooth. Cover the bowl and rest it at room temperature for at least one hour, or up to overnight in the refrigerator. Resting lets the starch granules hydrate fully and the gluten relax, giving the batter elasticity without toughness.

Preheat the oven to 230 C (450 F) — this is not a suggestion, it is the entire reason Yorkshire puddings rise. Place a 12-cup tin or a large roasting tray in the oven with a teaspoon of dripping in each cup (or a generous pool in the tray). Heat the fat in the oven for at least 15 minutes, until it is shimmering, smoking lightly, and loud — you must hear it spit when a drop of batter hits it. The fat must be violently hot: it flash-steams the batter's liquid into a jet of steam that drives the rise before the structure sets.

Working with decisive speed, remove the searingly hot tin from the oven and set it on a heatproof surface. Pour the batter from a jug into each cup, filling each about one-third full. The batter should sizzle and immediately begin to cook around the edges on contact with the fat. Return the tin to the oven instantly — every second of delay costs rise. Bake at 230 C (450 F) for 20–25 minutes. Do not open the oven door for the first 15 minutes under any circumstances: a cold rush of air is enough to collapse them.

fr-zabaglione: Place the egg yolks and caster sugar in a large, deep, round-bottomed metal or glass bowl. Whisk vigorously by hand or with a hand mixer until the mixture turns pale ivory, triples slightly in volume, and falls from the whisk in a thick, slow ribbon that holds its shape on the surface for 2-3 seconds before dissolving. This pre-mixing — called 'blanchir' — begins the emulsification and ensures even, smooth cooking over the bain-marie. The sugar must be nearly fully dissolved before the bowl goes over heat — feel the mixture between fingers; it should feel smooth, not gritty.

Add the Marsala wine to the ribboned yolk-sugar mixture and whisk to combine. The mixture will thin out significantly — this is expected. The Marsala should be at room temperature; cold wine can cause the eggs to cook unevenly. Taste the raw mixture: it should be sweet, winey, and slightly rich. This is your baseline — everything that follows is just cooking and incorporating air.

Bring a saucepan of water to a gentle simmer — the water must not touch the bottom of the bowl, and it must not boil aggressively. Place the bowl of zabaglione base over the simmering water and immediately begin whisking continuously in a figure-eight pattern, making sure to reach the sides and bottom of the bowl. Whisk without stopping for 8-12 minutes. The mixture will slowly begin to thicken, increase dramatically in volume, and change from liquid to a thick foam. Watch the temperature: if you see any steam rising from the mixture or the eggs begin to look lumpy at the edges, remove the bowl from the heat immediately and continue whisking off-heat for 30 seconds, then return. The target temperature is 70-75 C (160-170 F). The zabaglione is done when it has tripled in volume and holds a soft mound.

Divide the warm zabaglione immediately among warm glasses or shallow coupes — it will begin to deflate and separate within 10-15 minutes, so speed matters. Spoon the fresh berries or sliced peaches alongside or beneath the foam. The warm foam against cold or room-temperature fruit is the defining contrast of the dish. Serve with a small spoon and delicate gluten-free biscuits, such as gluten-free sponge fingers, if desired. Zabaglione can also be chilled briefly and served cold, in which case fold in a small amount of softly whipped cream while it is still warm to stabilize the foam.
